title: Shared Item-Level Error Limits the Aggregation of Small Language Models in Fermi Estimation
trick: Split each answer's log error into the model's mean error on that item plus a draw residual; averaging or debating only shrinks the residual, and the item part is 91% of the variance.
framing_stripped: Called 'shared item-level error limits aggregation' with 'four research questions' on structure, aggregation, communication and interventions; it is a one-way analysis of variance by item on 2.51M $\log_{10}$ errors from 15 open-weight models (3B-72B) answering 529 realFP Fermi questions about 350 times each at $T = 0.4$ (Table 1, App. B), which finds the intraclass correlation $\rho = A/(A+B)$ is a median 0.906 (so a team of 30 is worth $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.10$ independent draws, sec. 4.1), plus two simulated references that bracket what averaging could ever recover (sec. 3.2), a within-subject debate control showing three rounds collapse disagreement by 93% and move $A$ by $-0.9$% (sec. 6), and a screen of interventions (model mixing, prompts, temperature, activation edits, recalibration) scored by whether they lower $A$ and the team error together (sec. 7, Table 4); the paper is a measurement with a negative result for teams and a conditional one for interventions.
method_equations: Decomposition (eq. 1, sec. 3.1): for a fixed model and benchmark, draw $k$ on item $j$ with true value $y_j$ and estimate $\hat{y}_{jk}$ has signed error in orders of magnitude (OOM) $e_{jk} = \log_{10} \hat{y}_{jk} - \log_{10} y_j$, written $$e_{jk} = \mu + c_j + u_{jk}, \qquad \mathbb{E}_j\, c_j = 0, \qquad \mathbb{E}[u_{jk} \mid j] = 0,$$ where $\mu$ is the model's overall bias, $\mu + c_j$ its mean error on item $j$ (shared by every draw of that model on that item), and $u_{jk}$ the residual of one draw. The conditioning set is (model, item): moments are 'taken over the items of the benchmark and the draws on each item' and the decomposition is fitted per model ('Fix a model and a benchmark'); the run (prompt version, three runs per model) is a further shared component estimated separately (App. D, Table D.2, 'run (%)': 0.0-10.6%). Variance components (eq. 2): $$A = \operatorname{Var}_j(c_j), \qquad B = \mathbb{E}_j \operatorname{Var}(u_{jk} \mid j), \qquad \rho = \frac{A}{A+B}, \qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}(N) = \frac{N}{1 + (N-1)\rho},$$ with $A$ the between-item variance of the item-mean error, $B$ the average within-item variance, $\rho$ the intraclass correlation of draws over items, and $N_{\mathrm{eff}}(N)$ the number of independent draws with the same mean squared error over items as a team of $N$ (Kish's design effect). Team error (sec. 3.1, 'What aggregation can remove'): for any combining rule $g$ that shifts with its inputs, $g(x + a) = g(x) + a$ (mean, median, trimmed mean), the team error on item $j$ is $$\mu + c_j + g(u_{j1}, \ldots, u_{jN}),$$ so the item-level error passes through unchanged; for the geometric mean with draws independent given the item the expected squared error over items is $\mu^2 + A + B/N$, and $\mu^2 + A$ is a floor for every such rule but not for procedures using information beyond the answers (a recalibration learned on labelled items) or that change the agents. Estimation (sec. 3.1, App. D): $A$ and $B$ by one-way decomposition by item of round-1 draws, errors winsorized at $\pm 5$ OOM, $A$ corrected for the sampling variance of the item means; a second estimate from the fit $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{e}_N) = A + B/N$ to real team means. Metric (sec. 3.4): $\mathrm{MAE@5} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \min(|e|, 5)$; correct to the order of magnitude if $|e| \leq 0.5$, catastrophic if $|e| > 2$; team estimate is the geometric mean so its signed error is the mean of the members'; item is the unit of inference, 95% item-clustered bootstrap intervals. References (sec. 3.2): 'resampled given the item' draws each member with replacement from the model's round-1 errors on the same item (about 350 per item); 'unbiased given the item' is the same with independent random signs, removing $\mu + c_j$ while keeping magnitudes. Dispersion $D$ is the median over items of the within-team interquartile range; $W$ the within-team variance. Observed (Table 2, realFP main): $\rho$ one-way 0.906 (range over models in Table D.2: 0.789-0.986), team-fit 0.922; $N_{\mathrm{eff}}(30) = 1.08$ median (1.10 in text); same-model single-draw correlation 0.906, different-model 0.591 ($N_{\mathrm{eff}}(30) = 1.65$); per-item mean errors of two models correlate 0.827 Pearson (105 pairs), 0.64-0.67 robust, 0.60-0.69 with the linear magnitude trend removed; teammates' residuals against the item-and-run mean correlate $-0.010$ to $+0.032$; real team of 30 minus resampled-given-item reference $+0.005$ OOM; reduction at $N = 30$: real 1.7% median / 5.4% max, unbiased-given-item reference 74-79%, share realised 2.2% / 7.1%; $\sqrt{A} = 2.64$ OOM at round 1 and round 3 of debate, $D$ 0.211 to 0.014 OOM ($-93$%), $W$ $-20$%, team error 2.281 (one agent) to 2.251 (five aggregated) to 2.233 OOM (after debate), 2.1% total at fifteen times the generation cost (sec. 6); self-revision vs genuine peers at round 3: $+0.008$ $[-0.002, +0.017]$ OOM (realFP), $+0.015$ $[+0.003, +0.026]$ (SciOly) (Table 3). Compression (sec. 4): slope of per-item median signed error on $\log_{10} y$ from $-0.21$ to $-0.48$, all 15 negative, median crossing $10^{6.3}$, explaining 17% (6-29%) of $A$. Interventions (Table 4): mixture of five similar models vs their own teams $-0.142$ $[-0.191, -0.095]$ OOM (6.6%), vs best member's team $-0.035$ $[-0.117, +0.046]$; 0 of 4,928 mixtures significantly better than the best homogeneous team; per-agent scaffolds $-0.104$ $[-0.196, -0.015]$, $\Delta A = -10$%, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}} = 0.089$; calculator offload $+0.540$ $[+0.363, +0.720]$; $T = 1.0$ vs $0.4$: $-0.005$ $[-0.024, +0.013]$, $\Delta A$ $-4$%, $B$ up similarly; layer-14 skipping (qwen2.5-7b, 150 items) $-0.276$ $[-0.431, -0.126]$, $\Delta A$ $-11$%; linear recalibration $\log_{10} y \approx a + b\bar{x}_j$ (10-fold CV, least absolute deviations) team-of-30 gain 4.3% of single-agent error vs 1.5% without, $\Delta A = +0.5$%, fitted $b < 1$.
load_bearing_assumption: That the per-(model, item) mean error $\mu + c_j$ is a property of the model-and-item pair that no answer-combining rule can touch, so that $\mu^2 + A$ is a real floor rather than an artefact of how the draws were generated. The decomposition conditions on model and item but the draws all come from one predictive distribution under one prompt at $T = 0.4$, top-$p = 0.95$, 1024 new tokens, thinking off ('in round 1 every member of a team receives the same prompt, without exemplars or peer content, so a homogeneous team is $N$ samples from one predictive distribution', sec. 3.3; Table 1). What is called 'item-level' is therefore everything constant across draws under that sampling regime: the model's belief about the item, the prompt template's effect on the item, the decoding truncation, and label error, undivided. The paper tests the two cheapest of these and finds them small (temperature to 1.0 moves $A$ by $-4$%, Table 4; label audit flags 5.5% of items and removing them changes the cross-model mean error per item by 5.3%, App. C) and says plainly that the correlations 'do not identify the cause' (sec. 4.1), but the arms that would test the rest, 'extended test-time reasoning, which our token budget excludes, and item-specific information, such as retrieval of reference values for each factor' (sec. 8), are untested. If $c_j$ shrinks substantially under thinking mode or a larger token budget, the headline is about short-budget small models, not about aggregation. The second load-bearing piece is that the geometric mean (and median, App. E) is the aggregation rule of interest: rules that use the answers' spread or confidence fields (CONF 0-100 is requested in every prompt, App. A, and never used in the analysis) are shift-equivariant only if they ignore that information.
weakest_component: The thing a critic attacks first is the decoding regime that defines the within-item residual: every main-sweep draw is at $T = 0.4$ with thinking disabled and 1024 new tokens, so $B$ is the spread of a deliberately narrow sampler and $\rho = 0.906$ is partly a statement about the sampler. The paper's own temperature sweep (four models, three of one family, one run, $T \leq 1$) finds $A$ falls 3-4% and $B$ rises by a similar amount with team error unchanged (sec. 7), and the authors list the sweep's narrowness as a limitation; no run uses thinking mode, which the discussion names as one of two untested routes (sec. 8). Second, the main sweep mixed two prompt pairs unevenly across models (41% of round-1 answers from the revised pair, across 8 models), identified after the fact from prompt length because 'the run manifests do not record the prompt pair' (App. B); the revised pair is $-0.20$ OOM $[-0.24, -0.15]$ better, and the shared run deviation is up to 11% of error variance in 6 models (sec. 4.1), so per-model accuracy and bias levels and their ranks are, by the paper's own statement, prompt-dependent. Third, rounds 2 and 3 were generated by a parser that misread mantissa-times-power-of-ten answers, so in 22.5% of homogeneous and 32.6% of heterogeneous teams an agent saw a peer value that differed from what the peer wrote (sec. 6); the heterogeneous-debate result is withdrawn and the SciOly peers-vs-self-revision difference loses significance after exclusion. Fourth, the intervention screen is mostly exploratory: only six prompt-level arms are confirmatory, the pre-specified plan 'was not registered publicly' (sec. 3.4), the one arm that lowers $A$ and the team (layer skipping) is one model on 150 items with the old parser and median rule, and per-agent anchors are confounded with model identity (Table 4 note). Fifth, benchmark validity: SciOly's answer key records only the power of ten so an exactly right answer carries an error in $[0, 1)$ that enters $\mu$ and $c_j$; Guesstimate has 15 items; realFP has 29 of 529 items flagged where the models agree and the key disagrees by $\geq 1.5$ OOM, 'most others are ill-posed' (App. C).
regime: Models: 15 instruction-tuned open-weight models from nine lineages, 3.1B-72.7B (qwen2.5-3b, smollm3-3b, qwen3-4b, mistral-7b, olmo2-7b, qwen2.5-7b, llama3.1-8b, marin-8b, qwen3-8b, phi4-14b, qwen3-14b, gpt-oss-20b [3.6B active], qwen3.6-27b, llama3.3-70b-awq, qwen2.5-72b-awq; the two largest are AWQ 4-bit), served in bf16 through vLLM (activation screen: HuggingFace transformers); r1-distill-qwen-14b excluded for hitting the token limit on 66-85% of generations (Table B.1). Sampling: $T = 0.4$ (temperature sweep also 0.8 and 1.0), top-$p = 0.95$, 1024 new tokens (512 in the activation screen), thinking modes disabled (Table 1). Tasks: realFP 529 items with positive finite answers from $10^{-29}$ to $10^{90}$ (middle half $10^{1.8}$-$10^{7.6}$); SciOly 500 items (answer key is a power of ten only); Guesstimate 15 items (counts 13-382). Protocol: team sizes $N \in \{2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30\}$, three runs, 117 agent slots per run, about 350 round-1 draws per model per item, 2.51M round-1 answers in the main sweep; rounds 2-3 show peers' FINAL, CONF and 120 tokens of text (App. A); horizon is one answer per round, three rounds. Pass bands: a single agent is within one order of magnitude on 12-34% of realFP items and off by more than $100\times$ on 30-63% (Table 2); pooled median $|e|$ 1.86, mean 3.65, max 142 OOM (sec. 3.4); single-agent MAE@5 ranges from 1.628 (gpt-oss-20b) to about 3 OOM (llama3.1-8b 2.99 under the original prompt, Table B.2); five models of similar accuracy have MAE@5 2.08-2.32. Dates: answers up to 21 July 2026 used the original prompt pair, from 23 July 2026 the revised one (App. B); arXiv 2026-11-12, v1; cs.MA, cs.AI; venue not stated. GPU-hours, dollar cost, code release: unknown (not in text) except 'a complete rerun reproduces them exactly' from scored answers (sec. 8).
information_asymmetry: (1) Hindsight vs deployment. The floor $\mu + c_j$ is known only in hindsight, from about 350 draws per (model, item) against the answer key; at deployment a team has $N \leq 30$ draws on one item and no key, and every shift-equivariant rule returns $\mu + c_j + g(u)$ (sec. 3.1). What the team does hold and the analysis discards is the per-item spread of its $N$ draws (an estimate of $\operatorname{Var}(u_{jk} \mid j)$) and the CONF 0-100 field every prompt demands (App. A). Whether spread or confidence predicts $|c_j|$ is in the data and not reported; if it does, a team can flag its own floor. (2) One model vs the pool. Given one model $\rho = 0.906$; across models the single-draw correlation is 0.591 and per-item mean errors correlate 0.60-0.69 after the magnitude trend (sec. 4.1), so about a third of one model's item component is model-specific. Which model is wrong on which item exists in the pooled corpus and is used only to score mixtures, never to weight members per item (sec. 7). (3) FINAL vs RATIONALE. Every answer carries a factor list (revised prompt, App. A); only FINAL is analysed. Which factor carries $c_j$ (a shared constant, a dropped power of ten, the compression toward $10^{6.3}$) is in the text and undecomposed; calculator offload shows factor choice, not arithmetic, is at fault (sec. 7). (4) Sampler vs agent. $B$ is measured at $T = 0.4$, thinking off, 1024 tokens; extended reasoning and per-factor retrieval, the two routes that change $c_j$, are untested (sec. 8). For the lane: a three-way attribution (item given model, model, draw) plus a run component, saying the draw that debate and voting act on is 9% of the variance; the open port is the same decomposition on a discrete agent benchmark under pass^k, where 'item-level error' becomes 'the task failed on every seed'.
occupies: Published: on realFP, SciOly and Guesstimate under one prompt pair, 15 open-weight 3B-72B models at $T = 0.4$ with thinking off, the one-way variance decomposition of $\log_{10}$ error by item with $\rho = 0.906$ / 0.887 / 0.763, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}(30) \approx 1.1$; teammates' residuals uncorrelated given item and run ($-0.010$ to $+0.032$) and real teams matching the resampled-given-item reference to $+0.005$ OOM; teams of 30 recovering 1.7% (max 5.4%) of single-agent error against 74-79% for the unbiased-given-item reference; universal magnitude compression toward $10^{6.3}$ explaining 17% of $A$; cross-model per-item error correlation 0.60-0.69 after the trend, same-family not more correlated; three debate rounds cutting dispersion 93% with $A$ unchanged and self-revision matching peers; model mixing +6.6% over own teams and 0 of 4,928 mixtures beating the best model; temperature to 1.0 moving team error by about 1% at most; contrastive steering null; per-agent scaffolds and layer-14 skipping as unestablished candidates; cross-validated linear recalibration removing $\mu$ but not $c_j$. Not claimed and left open: any thinking-mode or long-budget run; any frontier or closed model; retrieval of per-factor reference values alone (only combined with calculator offload); a clean heterogeneous-debate test (parser defect); use of the CONF field or within-team spread to predict the item-level error; the same decomposition on discrete agent benchmarks.

neighbors.title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
neighbors.trick: Define a chance-corrected agreement score on which items two models get wrong, show judges favour similar models and weak-to-strong gains need complementary errors, and find mistakes grow more similar as capability rises; this paper cites it for 'correlated errors across language models on discrete benchmarks' and moves the measurement to a continuous scale where the common component is in the units of the answer (sec. 1, 2).

neighbors.title: Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?
neighbors.trick: Split multi-agent debate into majority voting and the exchange, show voting carries most of the gain on seven benchmarks, and prove debate is a martingale over beliefs so it cannot raise expected correctness without a biased update; this paper's self-revision control reaches the same conclusion on a continuous task ('consistent with reports that the exchange between agents adds little beyond voting', sec. 6).

neighbors.title: Understanding Agent Scaling in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems via Diversity
neighbors.trick: Bound multi-agent performance by task uncertainty and the number of effective information channels, so homogeneous agents saturate early while two diverse agents match sixteen identical ones, with a label-free channel count $K^*$; this paper names it among studies that 'identify the correlation between agents as the limit' and answers in variance units, finding mixing gains 6.6% but no mixture beats the best model (sec. 2, 7).

neighbors.title: Representational Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Committees: Measurement and Diversity-Aware Consensus
neighbors.trick: Embed each committee agent's rationale, measure cosine similarity (0.888) and effective rank (2.17 of 3) across role-prompted copies of one model, and weight votes by embedding diversity; this paper cites it as agreement measured 'in representation space' and instead measures the shared component directly as error on the item (sec. 2).

neighbors.title: More Agents Is All You Need
neighbors.trick: Sample many answers and majority-vote them, and show accuracy rises with the number of agents across benchmarks, more so on harder tasks; this paper is the counter-case: on Fermi items the gain from more agents of one model is 1.7% at $N = 30$ because the draws share the item error (sec. 1, 5).

theme_fit.why: directly attributes outcome variance to who moved (item given model 0.906, draw 0.094, run up to 0.11, model-specific share about a third of the item component) with the conditioning set written out, and shows where the aggregation and debate arguments fail in the units of the answer; it is an instrument (two simulated references plus the $A$-and-team criterion for interventions) with a small recipe consequence, and the discrete-benchmark port is a solo, sub-GPU-week probe
same words (multi-agent, debate, self-correction) but no training and no credit signal; it supplies the null that debate acts on the residual only, useful as a baseline for multi-agent RL claims
one cost sentence (debate's 2.1% gain 'at fifteen times the generation cost', sec. 6) and nothing on serving; cost is counted in generations, never in tokens or dollars
peers' answers are a 120-token message but nothing is measured about the handoff itself

limitations_as_complaints: My headline floor is measured under one narrow sampler and I cannot say how much of it is the sampler: all draws are at '$T = 0.4$ ... with top-$p = 0.95$, 1024 new tokens ... and thinking modes disabled' (Table 1); 'the temperature sweep covers four models (three of one family), one run and $T \leq 1$' (sec. 8); 'frontier, closed and reasoning models were not tested' and 'extended test-time reasoning, which our token budget excludes' is one of the 'two routes [that] remain untested' (sec. 8), so I do not know whether the item-level component survives thinking mode or a larger budget.

My correlations say the models err together on the same items but not why: 'These are correlations of errors ... They do not identify the cause. Shared knowledge acquired from similar text, properties of the items and their construction, and errors in the answer key would all produce them' (sec. 4.1); my label audit flags 5.5% of items and 'most others are ill-posed' (App. C); 'SciOly's answer key offsets its signed errors, and Guesstimate has 15 items' (sec. 8); and I collected a CONF field and a factor-by-factor RATIONALE on every answer (App. A) that the analysis never uses to locate the shared error.

My debate data are partly corrupted and my intervention screen is mostly exploratory: 'Rounds 2 and 3 were generated with a defective parser (Section 6); a definitive test of heterogeneous debate requires regenerating them'; 'the activation screen covers one model, 150 items and the median rule, and its model is recorded in the job configuration rather than in the stored results; $A$ is sensitive to winsorization when an arm inflates the spread'; 'Only the six prompt-level arms form a confirmatory family' (sec. 8), the plan 'was not registered publicly' (sec. 3.4), and 'the main sweep mixes two prompt pairs unevenly across models' so 'per-model levels of accuracy and bias, and their rank correlations, are prompt-dependent' (sec. 8).

history.note: W46 weekly run; evidence_level full-text (arxiv.org/html/2611.16315, LaTeXML, 8 sections plus appendices A-H, read via tag-stripped text; seed abstract and metadata from data/seeds/2026-W46.jsonl; five neighbour abstracts via one export.arxiv.org API id_list call; Kim et al. 2025 'Correlated errors in large language models' and Chuang et al. 2025 are positioned against in the text but carry no arXiv id there and were not fetched); lane context L1 (zero open claims this week; lane cares about attributing variance to who moved and where aggregation/debate arguments fail): decomposition is per item given the model with run as a separate shared component, sampling T=0.4 top-p 0.95 1024 tokens thinking off, and the paper states it cannot separate shared knowledge, item construction and label error as causes of the item-level component
